title: Better than a bot – instilling ethical judgement into the lawyers of the future in the age of AI

st.t: Machine judging: Accuracy cannot establish legitimate authority
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core distinction between technical prediction and legitimate human judgement, arguing that AI output remains only one input into ethically constrained professional decision-making. It materially extends the proposition by identifying a developmental risk—automation may remove formative junior tasks—and calling for stronger education and reflective practice to preserve human judgement.
qs: Law schools and the various sectors of the legal profession – law firms, the Bar, corporate, government and not-for-profit sectors – need to redouble efforts to provide education and experiences to cultivate ethical judgement.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: Legg accepts the cluster’s core copilot proposition: AI may automate legal tasks, but human lawyers retain practical and ethical judgment. He materially extends it by proposing experiential education and career-long reflective practice to preserve judgment as automation removes traditional junior learning opportunities. He does not substantially address verification costs or confidentiality controls.
qs: Legal decision making will remain with human lawyers who must exercise judgement and ethics.

In legal practice, where AI will be adopted and tasks automated, individual lawyers and the entities that they work within, could employ self-reflection to a greater extent to make the most of available learning experi­ ences and advance ethical judgement.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s human-led, task-decomposition account and materially extends it by identifying ethical judgement, sensitivity to human consequences and duties to the administration of justice as irreducible elements of legal work that technology cannot be assumed to supply.

kp.d: Legg argues that client demands for efficiency and convenience and providers’ pursuit of competitive advantage drive AI adoption. He describes legal work as decomposable into tasks, with generative AI assisting research, drafting, contract review and summarisation. He expects competitive pressures to require cost savings to be passed on to clients; this is an economic argument rather than a reported measurement of pricing changes.
qs: Market forces are driving the increased adoption of technology in legal practice.
The clients of lawyers want efficiency and convenience.
AI tools will be able to draft memos, letters, contracts, client updates and presentations.
AI can also review contracts for legal issues and compliance with an entity’s standard clauses or policies.

kp.k: Automation exposure estimate concerns tasks, not lawyer job losses
kp.d: Legg cites Goldman Sachs’s 2023 estimate that AI could automate 44 per cent of current legal work tasks, compared with an all-industry average of 25 per cent. The figure is a cited estimate of potential task automation, not an observed displacement rate or a forecast that 44 per cent of lawyers will lose their jobs.
qs: Goldman Sachs has estimated that 44 per cent of current legal work tasks could be automated by AI (the average for all industries is 25 per cent).

kp.k: Professional duties may require appropriate AI use
kp.d: Legg argues conditionally that duties of competence and acting in clients’ best interests may require AI adoption where it improves quality or efficiency. Drawing on Australian solicitors’ obligations and citing the New York State Bar Association’s 2024 report, he also argues that manually performing tasks that AI greatly accelerates can lead to unethical billing or overcharging. This is not a blanket requirement to use AI for every task.
qs: If AI can improve the quality and/or efficiency of the lawyer’s work as outlined above then it may need to be used because it is in the client’s interest to do so.
Further, AI can save so much time that lawyers would be unethical to bill for doing these tasks manually.
Failure to use technology may result in overcharging.
The requirement of competence may be viewed as including delivering legal services with technology where appropriate.

kp.k: AI outputs do not replace professional judgement
kp.d: Legg’s central argument is that AI separates prediction and information production from deciding what action to take. He allows for AI products substituting for commoditised services, but maintains that broader client objectives and contextual considerations still require human judgement. This is a conceptual argument supported by cited scholarship, not a new empirical test of AI’s limits. Human checking of AI predictions is an additional safeguard against hallucinations, rather than the entirety of judgement.
qs: However, AI does not replace the lawyer’s exercise of professional judgement.
Even with the most advanced AI, the AI output is one factor in a larger matrix of issues and considerations.
There is still a decision to be made about how to use the AI output and what actions to take that will be guided by the larger picture of a client’s objectives.
Humans must use judgement to determine what to do with the predictions.

kp.k: Judgement integrates expertise, context, emotions and independence
kp.d: Legg characterises ethical judgement as multi-faceted, practical and wholistic: lawyers combine legal expertise, experience, ethics and emotional intelligence to address client problems under uncertainty. Drawing on Kronman, he emphasises empathy combined with detachment; lawyers must understand clients without allowing identification with their objectives to override prudent and lawful advice.
qs: Judgement is often required when there is uncertainty and partial information.
Emotions contain information.
Anthony Kronman argues that good lawyering judgement is the ability to be empathetic and detached at the same time.
Empathy is the ability to see things from someone else’s perspective without necessarily sharing or endorsing that viewpoint or concern.

kp.k: Judgement requires managing biases and real-time decisions
kp.d: Reporting Kiser’s work on overconfidence and confirmation bias and Kahneman’s distinction between fast and slow thinking, Legg argues that lawyers need both deliberate analysis and intuition. Some courtroom decisions must be immediate; reflective practice can help lawyers prepare for these situations and learn from decisions made quickly. He does not claim that slower analysis is always feasible or that intuition can simply be eliminated.
qs: System 1 is thinking fast with intuition and heuristics, while system 2 is slow, analytic, data-based and comprehensive.
However, thinking fast, or intuitive thinking, is an important part of lawyers’ judgement.
This is because some decisions must be made in real-time or immediately.
A classic example for lawyers are judgements in relation to witness examination or objections as to evidence in court.

kp.k: Public duties distinguish lawyers from AI tools
kp.d: Legg identifies lawyers’ obligations to justice, clients, independence and integrity as a central distinction from AI. Grounded in Australian case law and the Australian Solicitors’ Conduct Rules, his argument places the administration of justice above inconsistent client demands. He extends this responsibility beyond litigation to counselling, compliance and transactions, including in-house and government practice, where commercial or organisational pressures cannot override it.
qs: As explained below the lawyer has obligations to the administration of justice, the client and to their own personal independence and integrity that do not apply to AI.
A solicitor’s duty to the court and the administration of justice is paramount and prevails to the extent of inconsistency with any other duty
Incentives or pressures for ‘commerciality’ or achieving corporate or government client objectives cannot override the paramount duty to the administration of justice.

kp.k: Ethical advice exceeds instrumental client problem-solving
kp.d: Legg reports debates over neutral partisanship and lawyers’ personal morality but adopts the position that professional duties to justice constrain client representation. He argues for recognising moral dimensions and consequences, advising clients accordingly and respecting client autonomy within professional limits. He also rejects the assumption that clients necessarily seek wrongdoing: lawyers can help willing clients understand and comply with the law.
qs: Professional and personal morality may differ, but professional morality is not equated with the client’s moral position and the lawyer has higher and overriding duties.
In some situations, a client refusing to follow advice may require the lawyer to cease to act.
The client will want to follow the law, and even do the right thing morally, but they may lack knowledge of what that is, or how to do so, or not appreciate the ramifications of their decisions.

kp.k: Automation threatens traditional junior learning opportunities
kp.d: Legg warns that automating formative tasks may remove experiences through which novice lawyers previously developed expertise. He consequently calls for law schools and legal workplaces across private practice, the Bar, corporate, government and not-for-profit sectors to strengthen education and experiential development. This is a prospective training concern, not a measured account of reduced junior hiring or a quantified skills deficit.
qs: But as some tasks are automated and no longer available for the novice lawyer to learn from,17 the junior lawyer must make the most of their experiences.
As AI continues to impact upon legal services, changes to lawyers’ education and training will be required.

kp.k: Reflection makes experience a deliberate learning process
kp.d: Legg recommends reflective practice as a technique for developing ethical judgement through formal education and practice. It involves examining intended goals, actual outcomes, contributing factors and alternative actions rather than treating task completion as the endpoint. Its purpose is to expose implicit assumptions, values and skills so lawyers can improve future decisions; the article develops this recommendation through existing educational and professional scholarship.
qs: Reflection is a process for learning from experiences.

Reflective learning is designed to make a person think about an experience or task from the perspective of what they have learned, how they can improve, or do better next time, and how to apply the learning to future tasks or situations.
The aim is to make explicit, as much as possible, what lies behind good ethical judgement.

kp.k: Law schools should combine doctrine, experience and reflection
kp.d: Legg treats doctrinal knowledge as necessary but insufficient for practical judgement. Clinics, actual-event case studies and simulations can expose students to client needs beyond legal questions; reflection then helps identify skill gaps, assumptions and ethical issues. He qualifies this approach by noting that teaching time truncates practical experiences and that judgement requires repeated exposure over time.
qs: Experiential learning allows for students to apply their learning and emerging judgement in a more practical and wholistic manner.
The student experiences the need to draw on more than just legal knowledge but also human skills.
Experiencing simulations of real world practice is beneficial, but they are limited by the time available for teaching.
It requires exposure to a variety of problem situations and repetitive practice.

kp.k: Supervision must develop lawyers, not merely review work
kp.d: Legg describes immersion and supervision as established professional-learning mechanisms: juniors observe senior lawyers, undertake increasingly complex work and receive instruction and feedback. He recommends supplementing these mechanisms with formal reflection, potentially supported by journals and discussions with peers or supervisors. Supervision also helps transmit ethical values and develop workplace cultures conducive to professional responsibility.
qs: Supervision is more than the allocation of work and review of the final product, it is also supporting, training and developing the junior lawyer.
Supervision requires time, commitment and planning.
The benefit of reflection is magnified and shared.
An openness to discussing and reflecting on ethical issues develops the junior lawyer’s individual professional responsibility, but it also facilitates ethical conduct in the practice environment.

kp.k: Reflective teams require supportive organisational cultures
kp.d: Legg proposes reflection during matters and team reviews after matters or significant steps. Questioning framing and assumptions may counter ethical fading, including when winning or retaining business displaces ethical consideration. He recognises time constraints and fears that admitting mistakes may affect remuneration or promotion; leadership endorsement, a learning-oriented culture and explaining business benefits can help support adoption.
qs: Reflection can also be adopted in relation to an entire matter or by an entire team.
The focus needs to involve introspection, what could ‘we’ or ‘I’ have done better, not just a focus on external forces.
Second is that identifying failings or mistakes is unpleasant and may impact remuneration and promotion.
Senior leaders need to provide their endorsement of the value of reflection and lifelong learning.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Legg predicts task-level automation and competitive pressure to adopt AI, while arguing that ethical professional judgement remains a human responsibility and that legal education must adapt.
pts.d: Michael Legg argues that AI can make constituent legal tasks faster and more thorough, including research, drafting, contract review and summarisation. He reports Goldman Sachs’s estimate that 44 per cent of current legal tasks could be automated, compared with 25 per cent across industries; this is an automation-potential estimate, not a prediction that 44 per cent of lawyers will lose their jobs. He expects competition to require firms, to some extent, to pass savings to clients. He also argues that duties of competence, client interests and appropriate charging may require AI use when it improves quality or efficiency. His account permits substitution for commoditised services, such as simple contracts or legal information, but treats AI as an input rather than a replacement for human judgement in broader legal services. Lawyers must decide what action to take, account for clients’ circumstances and uphold professional duties that do not apply to AI. Automation may remove formative tasks for junior lawyers, making deliberate development of ethical judgement more important. Legg proposes experiential education, immersion, supervision and greater use of reflective practice to preserve and deepen that learning.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The article supports its claims with an external automation estimate, cited AI research and product examples, professional rules and cases, and scholarship on judgement and education; it does not report an original AI experiment.
pts.d: For automation exposure, Legg cites Hatzius et al.’s 2023 Goldman Sachs report, page 7. For AI capabilities and productivity, he cites research including Choi et al. (2024), Chien and Kim (2024), and Schwarcz et al. (2025), alongside examples from Thomson Reuters, Microsoft and LexisNexis; he does not reproduce task-performance measurements from those studies. The competitive adoption and savings-pass-through arguments draw on technology and legal-market commentary, including Johnson (2023). The possible ethical requirement to adopt AI is a legal argument based on Australian Solicitors’ Conduct Rules rule 4, MAEK Pty Ltd v Ibrahim [2022] WASC 285 and the New York State Bar Association’s 2024 AI report. The distinction between AI predictions and human judgement draws on professional guidance and scholarship, including Agrawal et al., Legg and Bell, Kronman, and Luban and Millemann. The junior-learning concern references Thomson Reuters’s January 2025 associate-gap commentary. The reflective-practice proposal rests on educational and professional-development literature, including Dewey, Schon, clinical legal education scholarship and supervision research. These are cited foundations for Legg’s argument, not an article-specific demonstration that reflective practice offsets AI-related loss of training opportunities.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Legg describes ongoing and future change without a fixed adoption or displacement deadline; ethical adoption and educational benefits are conditional.
pts.d: The article belongs to the journal’s 2024 volume and was published online on 29 April 2025. It discusses AI capabilities already being incorporated into practice alongside prospective automation, without specifying a year by which automation or market adjustment will be complete. The reported 44 per cent figure concerns potential automation of current tasks and is not assigned a completion date. Appropriate use and actual improvements in quality or efficiency condition the argument that professional duties may require adoption. Human judgement remains necessary in Legg’s account because AI output must be interpreted within wider client objectives, uncertainty, human relations and legal and ethical obligations; checking output for hallucinations is an additional human responsibility. The training problem is expressed as a possibility as formative tasks are automated, not as a measured reduction in junior employment. Reflective practice is proposed across a lawyer’s career, with law school providing a beginning rather than complete preparation. Its implementation requires training, time, supervision, leadership support and a culture in which discussing mistakes does not simply threaten remuneration or promotion.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted changes affect firms and clients economically, juniors and educators through altered learning opportunities, and lawyers and society through the continuing importance of ethical judgement.
pts.d: Law firms face pressure to invest in AI, improve productivity and share savings to win or retain client work; clients may benefit from lower costs, convenience and more effective service. Users of commoditised services may receive an AI-based substitute, while clients with complex problems still need contextual advice and decisions in Legg’s account. Junior solicitors and barristers risk losing opportunities to learn through basic research, drafting and other formative tasks. Law schools, supervisors and senior practitioners therefore face a greater responsibility to develop judgement through experience, feedback and reflection. The proposed educational response extends to private-practice firms, the Bar, corporate legal departments, government and not-for-profit settings, rather than one firm-size segment. Corporate and government lawyers retain obligations to the administration of justice despite organisational pressure. The public is affected because lawyers’ independent ethical judgement safeguards legality, fairness and the rule of law; the article does not quantify an AI-driven access-to-justice outcome.
